claim_assessments.claim_text: Sonolysis has extensive bench‑scale data across simple solutions, groundwaters, AFFF, foam fractionate, and concentrated IDW, plus one groundwater field demonstration [S01; S04; S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04 reports bench-scale ultrasonication of PFOA/PFOS/6:2 FTS in MQ, SW, CW and of 1000× diluted AFFF and FF (and GW) (S04-E03,E04,E08). S06 reports bench-scale 700 kHz sonolysis of individual PFAS, AFFF, and concentrated, high‑TDS IDW (S06-E01,E05). S01 reports a field demonstration in 50‑L, 100‑L capacity reactors treating PFAS‑laden groundwater (S01-E04,E05). Together these match the stated range of matrices and scales.

claim_assessments.claim_text: EO evidence consists of a pilot‑scale FF–EO system on groundwater and landfill leachate [S03] plus a generic process‑scale LCA model of EO [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03 describes a pilot-scale treatment train with foam fractionation of PFAS‑contaminated groundwater and landfill leachate followed by EO of the PFAS-enriched foam/waters (S03-E01,E03,E07). S05 is a process‑level LCA of EO (and other technologies) for PFAS destruction in water (S05-E03,E08).

claim_assessments.claim_text: RAP plasma evidence here is bench‑scale on relatively simple PFOA/PFOS aqueous solutions [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02 treats lab-prepared aqueous PFOA and PFOS solutions at µg/L–mg/L in 30–100 mL batch RAP reactors with argon (S02-E03,E05–E07). No complex matrices are described in the provided text.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the provided studies, “destruction” is most often measured as parent‑compound loss; only some sonolysis work evaluates defluorination explicitly.
claim_assessments.rationale: S01 defines degradation efficiency as loss of parent PFAS concentration (S01-E02). S04 distinguishes parent degradation and defluorination, explicitly quantifying F− release for PFOS/6:2 FTS and AFFF/FF (S04-E05,E06). S06 discusses both loss of parent PFAS and defluorination, including fluoride release and stoichiometric yields for some PFAS (S06-E01,E05). Thus sonolysis work clearly evaluates defluorination; for RAP and EO, only parent loss/EOF are reported. The qualifier “only some sonolysis work” is somewhat vague but generally consistent.

claim_assessments.claim_text: High‑frequency ultrasound (typically 700 kHz) generates acoustic cavitation; bubble collapse creates localized hot spots with very high temperature and pressure that induce pyrolysis and radical reactions [S01; S04; S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E01,E02 describe ultrasonication using high‑frequency sound, cavitation, and localized hot spots (~5000 K, >1000 atm) producing radicals and pyrolysis. S06-E06 similarly describes high‑frequency ultrasound creating nanoscale cavities with ~5000 K microenvironments causing pyrolysis and PFAS destruction. S01-E01 references high‑frequency ultrasound mineralizing PFAS via cavitation. Frequency 700 kHz is specified repeatedly in S06 (e.g., S06-E01,E05).

claim_assessments.claim_text: The sonolysis configurations include: a 700 kHz, 1040 W, 1000 mL closed reactor and a 700 kHz, 250 W, 200 mL open reactor [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E01,E03,E04 describe a 700 kHz, 1040 W closed reactor; S06-E02 notes 1000 mL treated in the closed system and 200 mL in the open system; S06-E08 states 700 kHz, 250 W open system with 200 mL and power density 1250 W L⁻¹. These match the description.

claim_assessments.claim_text: A field mobile sonolysis system had two 50‑L chambers (total ~100 L capacity) treating highly contaminated groundwater in batch [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E05 and S01-E04 describe specialized 50‑L ultrasound reactors in a trailer, with total system capacity of 100 L, treating PFAS‑laden groundwater in batch mode.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Awoyemi et al. sonolysis feed matrices included PFOA, PFOS, and 6:2 FTS spiked into Milli‑Q, seawater, and creek water, as well as 1000× diluted AFFF and foam fractionate in those matrices and a natural groundwater [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E08 states PFOA, PFOS, and 6:2 FTS were spiked in SW and CW, and the abstract/methods (E08) plus E06 cover MQ, SW, CW. S04-E03,E04 describe 1000× diluted AFFF and FF in MQ, SW, CW and mention additional GW experiments (though not quantified). The combination matches the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06, deionized water, low‑TDS groundwater (388 mg/L), and high‑TDS groundwater (10.2 g/L) were used with seven PFAS individually and as a 24‑compound mixture [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E05 specifies testing 7 individual PFASs, a 24Mix, AFFF, and IDW in deionized water, low‑TDS GW (388 mg/L) and high‑TDS GW (10.2 g/L).

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06, a concentrated, high‑TDS IDW sample (1000 mL) was treated in the 700 kHz, 1040 W closed reactor and 41 PFAS were detected and evaluated for defluorination [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E05 states concentrated high‑TDS IDW was treated in 700 kHz–1040 W conditions and that treatment of IDW resulted in significant defluorination of 41 PFASs. S06-E02 and E01 give the 1000 mL closed system volume.

claim_assessments.claim_text: HFPO‑DA and 6:2 FTAB exhibited near‑stoichiometric fluoride release under sonolysis, indicating extensive defluorination [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E05 explicitly notes degradation of HFPO‑DA and 6:2 FTAB with near‑stoichiometric fluoride release, which directly supports the claim of extensive defluorination.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Field groundwater treated by ultrasound in S01 was PFAS‑laden groundwater from source‑zone conditions at contaminated sites [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E05 states the objective was to treat PFAS‑laden groundwater within source zones at impacted sites; S01-E04 reiterates treatment of highly contaminated groundwater within a source zone.

claim_assessments.claim_text: RAP used atmospheric radial plasma discharge operating with argon bubbling in small, batch aqueous systems [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E04 describes argon bubbling controls; S02-E01 mechanistic discussion refers to argon plasma; S02-E03,E07 describe batch plasma experiments. The term RAP (radial plasma discharge reactor) is used in multiple chunks (e.g., S02-E02,E06).

claim_assessments.claim_text: RAP experiments used laboratory‑prepared aqueous solutions of single PFAS in low volumes (30–100 mL) with no explicit co‑contaminants, salinity, or organic background, i.e., effectively clean matrices [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-R01/R02 records (summarized here) and S02-E03,E05,E07 specify 30 and 100 mL batch volumes and aqueous PFOA/PFOS solutions. No co‑contaminants, salinity, or background organics are mentioned in any provided S02 chunks, consistent with clean matrices.

claim_assessments.claim_text: RAP PFOA conditions included ~41–41.4 µg/L in 30 mL and 4.14–41.4 mg/L with volume up to 100 mL [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: The verification records for S02 (R01,R02) explicitly list initial PFOA concentrations of 41.4 µg/L in 30 mL and 4.14–41.4 mg/L in 30–100 mL batches (see operating_conditions and quantitative_findings).

claim_assessments.claim_text: RAP PFOS experiments used 5 mg/L PFOS in water [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-R03 and S02-E06 specify an initial PFOS concentration of 5 mg/L for energy-efficiency evaluation.

claim_assessments.claim_text: RAP transformation products from PFOA include PFHpA, PFHxA, PFPA, PFBA and minor polyfluorinated acids with partial H substitution [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E08 lists perfluoroheptanoic (PFHpA), perfluorohexanoic (PFHxA), perfluoropentanoic (PFPA), and other CnF2n+1COOH products, and notes additional minor polyfluorinated acids with one or two F replaced by H.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Lower‑homologue PFOS species (perfluoroheptane and perfluorohexane sulfonates) were present as impurities at time zero and were degraded, with no evidence of sulfonate chain‑shortening [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E01 states trace perfluoroheptane and perfluorohexane sulfonates were detected at time zero as impurities and were degraded; the authors note no evidence for sulfonate chain‑shortening via SO₃• in their system.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the FF–EO pilot, PFAS‑contaminated groundwater and landfill leachate had pH ~7.5–7.8, conductivity 450–470 mS/m, and TOC 2.1–2.7 mg/L [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E07 reports for the two raw waters a pH of 7.5–7.8, conductivity 450–470 mS/m and TOC 2.1–2.7 mg/L.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Foam fractionation in the pilot selectively enriched long‑chain PFAS in foam, leaving short‑chain PFAS in the de‑foamed effluent [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E01 notes FF is less efficient for short-chain/non-amphiphilic PFAS. S03-E07 reports long‑chain PFAA removal ≈90% while ΣPFAS removal was lower and attributes higher removal to higher adsorption coefficients of long‑chain PFAS. This supports selective enrichment of long‑chain PFAS in foam and poorer removal of short‑chain PFAS.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the pilot, average ΣPFAS removal by FF was 60% in groundwater and 51% in leachate, while long‑chain PFAA removal reached ~90% in both matrices [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E07 states mean ΣPFAS removal effectiveness was 60% (groundwater) and 51% (leachate), and removal of long‑chain PFAA reached approximately 90% in both water types.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Average recovery of influent ΣPFAS mass in FF effluent + foam was 87 ± 35% for groundwater and 58 ± 13% for leachate, indicating unaccounted PFAS fractions [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E07 reports average recoveries of influent ΣPFAS in effluent and foam of 87 ± 35% (groundwater) and 58 ± 13% (leachate), matching the claim.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the pilot EO step, EOF generally decreased after EO with magnitudes similar to target PFAS degradation and up to 44% EOF reduction in treated waters [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E03 notes that decreases in EOF after EO were similar to target PFAS degradation. S03-E08 reports extractable organofluorine decreased by up to 44% after the evaluated treatment technologies.

claim_assessments.claim_text: EO of PFSA in fractionated foam showed low electrochemical degradation [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E04 explicitly states that low electrochemical degradation of PFSA in fractionated foam was found and may challenge applicability of EO for PFAS‑enriched foam.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In waters containing chloride or bromide, EO can generate perchlorate, bromate, and toxic organic halides, posing an obstacle to industrial application [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E06 states that in water containing chloride or bromide at relevant concentrations, formation of perchlorate, bromate, and toxic organic halides is a concern and a substantial obstacle for industrial application.

claim_assessments.claim_text: The LCA treats EO as oxidizing PFAS in an aqueous conductive solution between anode and cathode via direct oxidation and indirect radical‑mediated pathways, with current lost to water electrolysis and oxidation of co‑contaminants [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-E05 describes EO as applying current through a conductive solution between anode and cathode, with direct oxidation via electron transfer and indirect radical generation; S05-E04 notes a substantial fraction of current is diverted to side reactions including water electrolysis and other species.

claim_assessments.claim_text: For PFOS and 6:2 FTS in seawater, degradation was very high (97% and 95%, respectively) but defluorination was only 2.3% and 4% [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E06 reports PFOS/6:2 FTS degradation efficiencies of 97%/95% in SW and defluorination efficiencies of 2.3%/4%, respectively.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In AFFF diluted 1000× (initial 2200 ppb PFAS), total PFAS reductions were ~60% in MQ, 54% in SW, and 83% in CW; in 1000× FF (1950 ppb), reductions were ~96% across MQ, SW, CW [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E03 gives initial total PFAS for AFFF (2200 ppb) and FF (1950 ppb) and post‑treatment values, showing approximate reductions of 60%, 54%, 83% for AFFF and 96%, 94%, 96% for FF in MQ, SW, CW respectively.

claim_assessments.claim_text: The AFFF vs FF reduction difference was attributed partly to higher initial PFAS in AFFF saturating the bubble surface and limiting cavitation [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E03 discusses that higher PFAS levels in AFFF may saturate the ultrasonic bubble surface, limiting cavitation and PFAS availability, and thereby lowering degradation efficiency compared to FF.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Treatment of concentrated, high‑TDS IDW (1000 mL) at 700 kHz, 1040 W resulted in significant defluorination of 41 PFASs with reported energy demand of “3 kWh g” (mass basis truncated) [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E05 states treatment of concentrated, high‑TDS IDW led to significant defluorination of 41 PFASs and consumed “3 kWh g…” (denominator not visible). S06-E01,E02 specify 700 kHz, 1040 W and 1000 mL volume.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In low‑TDS groundwater (388 mg/L), sonolytic degradation rates of sulfonates and short‑chain PFAS were 30–60% higher than in deionized water, whereas in high‑TDS groundwater (10.2 g/L) rates were lower [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E05 states degradation rates of sulfonates and short‑chain PFAS were 30–60% higher in low‑TDS GW (388 mg/L) than in deionized water, and that rates were lower in high‑TDS GW (10.2 g/L).

claim_assessments.claim_text: For diluted AFFF/FF, total PFAS reduction was systematically lower in seawater than in MQ or CW, which the authors attribute to high salinity inhibiting cavitation and scavenging radicals or forming stable complexes [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E03 notes reduction efficiency is lower in SW than in other waters and attributes this to high salinity possibly forming stable complexes or scavenging reactive radicals necessary for ultrasonication degradation.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In AFFF and IDW, PFAS constitute a small fraction of total organics; competitive adsorption to ultrasonic cavities and degradation of non‑fluorinated organics reduce PFAS‑specific degradation rates and complicate energy allocation [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E03 states PFASs in AFFF account for only 1–5% of total mass and that competitive adsorption to ultrasonic cavities can reduce PFAS degradation rates; S06-E02 notes unidentified organics in IDW also degrade and must be considered in energy estimates.

claim_assessments.claim_text: For IDW, energy metrics based solely on identified PFAS overestimate PFAS‑specific energy consumption; including unidentified PFAS and other organics lowers apparent energy per unit mass degraded but complicates interpretation [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E02 explains that accounting only for identified PFAS overestimates energy per mass PFAS, and that including unidentified PFAS and other degraded organics lowers apparent energy consumption but complicates performance assessment.

claim_assessments.claim_text: The field ultrasonic groundwater study monitored metals, anions, TOC, COD, PFAS TOP, and AOF and found little evidence of problematic PFAS by‑products among monitored species; gas‑phase intermediates were not characterized [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E02 lists analytes (PFAS, PFAS TOP, metals, anions including fluoride, TOC, COD, AOF). S01-E04 states the technology showed little evidence of problematic by‑products and recommends future research to evaluate gas‑phase intermediates to fully evaluate fluorine mass balance.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Batch sonolysis typically follows pseudo‑first‑order kinetics for PFAS degradation [S01; S04; S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E08 says ultrasound is a batch process that has demonstrated pseudo‑first‑order kinetics. S04-E06 models defluorination kinetics using (pseudo)-first‑order for F⁻ release. S06-E08 explicitly reports pseudo‑first‑order removal rate constants and notes they were determined from 240‑min experiments.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the 700 kHz, 250 W open system (200 mL), PFOA and PFOS pseudo‑first‑order rate constants were ~0.035 min⁻¹ and 0.0016 min⁻¹, respectively [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E08 reports PFOS k = 0.0016 ± 0.001 min⁻¹ and PFOA k = 0.035 ± 0.002 min⁻¹ in the 700 kHz, 250 W open system (power density 1250 W L⁻¹) over 200 mL.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the 1040 W closed sonolysis system, PFBS removal increased as power density was raised from 1040 to 5200 W/L, and atomization of the bulk liquid was observed at very high power density [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E03 describes PFBS removal rate increasing as power density increased from 1040 to 5200 W L⁻¹ and notes that atomization of the bulk liquid was observed in the 700 kHz, 1040 W closed system at high power density.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the closed sonolysis reactor, reaction mixture temperature increased to ~40 °C over 120 min and then stabilized despite cooling, indicating significant energy dissipation as heat [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E04 reports temperature rose steadily to ~40 °C over the first 120 min and remained constant over the next 120 min despite recirculation of 10 °C cooling water. This supports the temperature behavior; the specific interpretation that this indicates “significant energy dissipation as heat” is reasonable but not explicitly stated in the source.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In bench‑scale IDW sonication, significant defluorination required about “3 kWh g” of energy, although the mass basis in the unit is unknown [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E05 states treatment of concentrated, high‑TDS IDW resulted in significant defluorination of 41 PFASs, consuming 3 kWh g… (denominator truncated). The reviewer’s note about the unknown basis is consistent with the truncation.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the 1040 W closed reactor, inline metering recorded 0.4 kWh over 4 h, giving an estimated electricity cost of $0.18/gal at $0.12/kWh [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E04 reports an inline electricity meter showing 0.4 kWh consumed over four hours at 1040 W; it states that, assuming $0.12/kWh, the electricity cost was $0.18 per gallon.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the field groundwater ultrasound study, total power consumption per treatment cycle was 317 kWh, with power cost $1.57/gal ($0.41/L) at $0.15/kWh [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E08 states total power consumption per treatment cycle was 317 kWh and reports power cost $1.57/gal ($0.41/L) at $0.15/kWh.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In one field test (Test 2, Reactor 2), EEO for PFOA and PFOS were 2973 and 5572 kWh/m³/order respectively, and the authors caution these prototype EEOs may not reflect optimized performance [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E07 gives EEO values of 2973 and 5572 kWh/m³/order for PFOA and PFOS in Test 2, Reactor 2, and notes the reactor is a prototype and may not reflect true EEO at larger, more efficient scales; thus comprehensive EEO calculations are not presented.

claim_assessments.claim_text: At low PFOA concentration (~41.4 µg/L, 30 mL), RAP achieved ≥99% PFOA conversion in 2.5 min [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E05,E07 state that ≥99% PFOA conversion was achieved in less than 2.5 min for a 41–41.4 µg/L solution; S02-R01 reports treatment time of 2.5 min for ≥99% conversion.

claim_assessments.claim_text: RAP authors note that rapid treatment at low PFOA concentration is associated with higher specific energy costs, indicating a trade‑off between short reaction times and energy efficiency [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E07 states that trade‑off between short treatment times and high energy costs is an issue and that energy efficiencies as high as 2365 mg/kWh were achieved at higher concentration but with longer treatment times.

claim_assessments.claim_text: At higher PFOA concentration (41.4 mg/L), RAP achieved ≥99% conversion in 30 min with G50 as high as 2365 mg/kWh [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E05 and S02-E07 report ≥99% conversion in 30 min for 41 mg/L PFOA and energy efficiencies as high as 2365 mg/kWh at this concentration.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Increasing treated volume from 30 to 100 mL of a 4.14 mg/L PFOA solution did not compromise RAP process rate and achieved >99% degradation in 15 min with good energy efficiency [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E06 notes treatment of 100 mL aliquots of a 4.14 mg/L PFOA solution achieved >99% degradation in 15 min with a remarkable G50; S02-E07 states volume could be increased from 30 to 100 mL without compromising process rate while improving energy efficiency.

claim_assessments.claim_text: RAP degradation is modeled as pseudo‑first‑order, with half‑life t₁/₂ = ln2/k and t₀.₉ = ln2.3/k used for energy metrics G50 and EE/O [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E03 defines G50 using t1/2=ln2/k and EE/O using t0.9=ln2.3/k, indicating pseudo‑first‑order kinetics.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In RAP PFOA experiments, the sum of all detected organic products after 30 min accounted for only 6% of initial TOC, implying formation of undetected organic species and unquantified mineralization [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E08 states that the sum of detected degradation products after 30 min amounted to 6% of initial TOC as PFOA, suggesting formation of organic products undetected by the analysis.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In RAP PFOS experiments at 5 mg/L, G50 was 893 mg/kWh and EE/O was 4.51 kWh/m³, values reported as more energy‑efficient than PFOS plasma reactors in Mahyar et al. [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E06 reports G50=893 mg/kWh and EE/O=4.51 kWh/m³ at 5 mg/L PFOS and states the RAP reactor was at least 4 and 27 times more energy efficient than reactors used by Mahyar et al. However, the comparative descriptor to “PFOS plasma reactors in Mahyar et al.” is only partly grounded in the cited text; the numeric comparison is supported.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Groundwater and leachate FF raw waters had pH 7.5–7.8, conductivity 450–470 mS/m, and TOC 2.1–2.7 mg/L [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E07 provides this range for the two raw waters.

claim_assessments.claim_text: FF–EO pilot EOF and target PFAS degradation show that EO decreased EOF similarly to target PFAS, with up to 44% EOF reduction [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E03 states decrease in EOF after EO was similar to target PFAS degradation; S03-E08 mentions extractable organofluorine decreased by up to 44% after evaluated treatment technologies.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the EO discussion, high current densities can lead to mass‑transfer limitations, scale formation, and electrode fluorination, which can be reversed by acid rinsing or UV irradiation; staying in reaction‑limited regime via lower current density or enhanced mass transfer is more energy efficient but slower [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E06 notes scale formation creates mass-transfer limitations requiring acid rinsing, and that fluorination of BDD reduces rates but can be reversed by UV irradiation. It also says decreasing current density over time helps remain in reaction‑limited regime and can provide energy‑efficient degradation at cost of higher treatment times; high concentrations or turbulence-enhancing designs reduce mass-transfer issues.

claim_assessments.claim_text: An LCA using common functional units and TRACI categories found an integrated sustainability index of 0.90 for EO, 0.48 for UVAOP, and 0.29 for incineration under balanced weighting [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-E08 states EO had SI=0.90, UVAOP 0.48, incineration 0.29 under balanced environmental, economic, social weighting using MIVES and TRACI-based LCA.

claim_assessments.claim_text: The LCA notes that a substantial fraction of EO current is diverted to side reactions such as water electrolysis and oxidation of co‑contaminants, strongly affecting energy consumption and sustainability [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-E04 states not all electrical current goes toward contaminant degradation; a substantial fraction is diverted to side reactions such as water electrolysis or other species, influencing energy use and footprint.

claim_assessments.claim_text: No direct kWh per mass PFAS data are given for the pilot FF–EO in the supplied text, so quantitative energy comparison with sonolysis or RAP is not possible here.
claim_assessments.rationale: This is a statement about the absence of data in the excerpts. The S03 chunks/records provided do not report specific EO energy per mass PFAS, so the claim that such comparison is not possible within this evidence set is accurate.

claim_assessments.claim_text: The FF–EO treatment train decreased toxic potency of waters as measured by TTR binding (PFOS‑equivalent) and A. fischeri bioluminescence (triclosan‑equivalent) [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E02,E08 describe using TTR-binding and A. fischeri assays and expressing responses as PFOS- and triclosan-equivalents, but the provided text does not explicitly state that toxicity decreased. The existence of toxicity measurement is supported; the direction of change is not.

claim_assessments.claim_text: The FF–EO pilot observed that insufficient total applied EO energy density leads to PFAS being degraded mainly to shorter‑chain compounds rather than fully destroyed [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E06 states that if total applied energy density is not sufficient, PFAS are merely degraded to shorter‑chain compounds.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the FF–EO pilot, when chloride or bromide is present, EO can form perchlorate, bromate, and organic halides, necessitating toxicity evaluation of EO‑treated water [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E06 mentions formation of perchlorate, bromate, and toxic organic halides in chloride/bromide‑containing waters and emphasizes the importance of evaluating toxicity of electrochemically treated water.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the FF–EO study, EO reduced EOF and target PFAS such that it does not simply convert targeted PFAS to equally persistent, unmeasured PFAS at similar fluorine mass, although residual EOF remained [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E03 shows EOF decreased similarly to target PFAS, suggesting some broader organofluorine reduction, but it does not explicitly state that equally persistent unmeasured PFAS are not formed. The inference about not “simply converting” is interpretive.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the S01 field sonolysis study, average PFAS degradation efficiency reached 80% after 12 h, with about an order‑of‑magnitude decrease in PFAS concentration in highly contaminated groundwater and decreasing AOF [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E08 reports maximum average PFAS degradation efficiency of 80% at 12 h and shows decreasing AOF; S01-E04 describes an order‑of‑magnitude decrease in PFAS concentration and a decrease in AOF.

claim_assessments.claim_text: The S01 field sonolysis study did not achieve a closed fluorine mass balance; gas‑phase intermediates were not characterized [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E04 calls for future research to evaluate gas‑phase intermediate compounds to fully evaluate fluorine mass balance, implying it was not closed.

claim_assessments.claim_text: For seawater sonolysis, PFOS and 6:2 FTS show high parent loss but very low defluorination (2.3–4%), suggesting salts/ions influence radical pathways or facilitate escape of ultrashort‑chain intermediates [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: The numeric contrast between degradation and defluorination is supported (S04-E06). The hypothesis that salts/ions influence radical pathways or facilitate escape is consistent with S04-E02,E06 but is framed as suggested mechanisms by the authors; the reviewer’s causal language is slightly interpretive.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06, degradation rates in high‑TDS groundwater (~10.2 g/L) were lower than in low‑TDS groundwater [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E05 explicitly states degradation rates were lower in high‑TDS GW (10.2 g/L) compared to low‑TDS GW.

claim_assessments.claim_text: For AFFF and FF in seawater vs MQ/CW, total PFAS reduction was lower in SW, and authors attribute this to high salinity inhibiting cavitation and scavenging radicals or forming stable complexes [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E03 reports lower reduction efficiency in SW and attributes it to high salinity inhibiting effectiveness via possible formation of stable complexes or scavenging of reactive radicals.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06 IDW experiments, energy losses in conversion from electrical power to effective cavitation are very high, and energy efficiency is strongly influenced by matrix chemistry and ultrasound frequency; frequency optimization is compound‑specific and not practical for complex mixtures like IDW [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E07 states energy losses in converting electrical energy to cavitation are very high, suggests altering matrix chemistry to increase energy translation efficiency, and notes frequency optimization is compound‑specific and not practical for mixtures and actual waters.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06 IDW sonication, a substantial amount of co‑occurring organics is degraded along with PFAS, complicating attribution of energy consumption [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E02,E03 mention that PFAS constitute only 1–5% of total mass in AFFF and that various unidentified organics in IDW and AFFF are degraded, which should be included in energy calculations, complicating PFAS‑specific energy assessment.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S02 RAP low‑concentration PFOA tests (41–4100 µg/L), G50 values above 2000 mg/kWh were reported [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E05 notes G50 greater than 2000 mg/kWh for 41 µg/L–4.1 mg/L PFOA initial concentrations.

claim_assessments.claim_text: For PFOS RAP at 5 mg/L, G50 = 893 mg/kWh and EE/O = 4.51 kWh/m³, which the authors state are markedly more energy‑efficient than reactors in a comparative PFOS plasma study [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E06 reports these values and states RAP was at least 4× and 27× more energy efficient than reactors used by Mahyar et al., thus markedly more energy‑efficient.

claim_assessments.claim_text: For PFOA RAP, sequential formation and decay of PFHpA, PFHxA, PFPA, PFBA support a chain‑shortening pathway; after 30 min, identified products account for only 6% of initial TOC, with the rest in undetected organic species [S02].
claim_assessments.rationale: S02-E08 describes rising then falling profiles of PFHpA, PFHxA, and increasing PFPA, interpreting these as sequential chain‑shortening; it explicitly states detected products after 30 min sum to 6% of initial TOC, implying remaining carbon is in undetected organics.

claim_assessments.claim_text: The RAP evidence set does not report fluoride or CO₂, so defluorination and mineralization extents cannot be deduced.
claim_assessments.rationale: None of the S02 excerpts mention fluoride or CO₂ measurements. The statement that these endpoints are unreported and thus mineralization/defluorination are unknown is consistent with the evidence.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the pilot FF–EO, mean ΣPFAS removal by FF was 60% in groundwater and 51% in leachate, with long‑chain PFAA removal ~90%, and FF removed long‑chain PFAS more efficiently than short‑chain PFAS [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E07 provides the mean ΣPFAS removal values and notes that long‑chain PFAS were removed better than short‑chain PFAS, with long‑chain PFAA removal approximately 90%.

claim_assessments.claim_text: Average recoveries of influent ΣPFAS in FF effluent + foam were incomplete (87 ± 35% in groundwater, 58 ± 13% in leachate), indicating PFAS losses needing investigation before scale‑up [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E07 reports these recovery percentages and presents them as mass balance closure issues, which are a limitation for implementation.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the FF–EO study, extractable organofluorine in water decreased by up to 44% after the evaluated treatments [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E08 states that extractable organofluorine concentration decreased by up to 44% after the evaluated PFAS treatment technologies.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S03, unknown PFAS species contributed to EOF in most samples; after EO, EOF decreased similarly to target PFAS, but residual EOF remained and specific residual species were not identified [S03].
claim_assessments.rationale: S03-E03 notes higher EOF than explained by target PFAS, indicating unknown PFAS, and that EOF decreased similarly to target PFAS after EO while further analytical work would be needed to identify potential PFAS; it implies residual EOF remains.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S04 seawater sonolysis, high PFOS/6:2 FTS degradation but low defluorination suggests formation or escape of ultrashort‑chain PFAS intermediates and complex interactions with salts and ions; authors note the pathway is complicated and needs further research [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E06 makes exactly this point: it contrasts high degradation with low defluorination and suggests possible formation/escape of ultrashort-chain intermediates or interactions with salts/ions, and explicitly states the degradation pathway is complicated and requires more research.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S04, ultrasonication of AFFF and FF produced mainly short‑chain PFAS; multiple lines of evidence suggest these short‑chain PFAS are generally less toxic than long‑chain PFAS, but they remain organofluorine residues.
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E03 states ultrasonication produced mainly short‑chain PFAS and cites evidence that they have lower toxicity than long‑chain PFAS. The additional comment that they “remain organofluorine residues” is inferential rather than directly stated.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S04, HF potentially produced during ultrasonication was captured as mist via a vacuum system and NaOH scrubber, indicating HF as a likely inorganic by‑product [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E04 describes mist potentially containing HF being captured into ~0.1 M NaOH via a vacuum flow system, implying HF generation.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06, high‑frequency ultrasound of various PFASs produced near‑stoichiometric fluoride release for HFPO‑DA and 6:2 FTAB and significant defluorination of 41 PFASs in IDW [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E05 reports near‑stoichiometric fluoride release for HFPO‑DA and 6:2 FTAB and significant defluorination of 41 PFASs in concentrated IDW.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S04, 1000× diluted AFFF and FF ultrasonication produced total PFAS reductions of ~54–83% (AFFF) and ~94–96% (FF) depending on matrix [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E03 gives initial and final PFAS values for AFFF and FF in MQ, SW, CW, corresponding to ~60,54,83% reductions for AFFF and ~96,94,96% for FF.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06, pseudo‑first‑order rate constants for PFOA and PFOS in the 700 kHz, 250 W open system were 0.035 ± 0.002 min⁻¹ and 0.0016 ± 0.001 min⁻¹, respectively [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E08 provides these kinetic constants for PFOA and PFOS in the open system.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06, PFAS removal rates decreased with decreasing power density; PFBS removal increased as power density increased from 1040 to 5200 W/L but atomization was observed at very high power density, potentially limiting operation [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E03 states removal rates decreased with decreasing power density, PFBS removal increased with power density from 1040 to 5200 W L⁻¹, and atomization of bulk liquid was observed. The inference that atomization “potentially limits operation” is not explicitly in the text.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06, energy losses during conversion of electrical energy to ultrasound cavitation are very high, motivating approaches like matrix optimization or process coupling to reduce energy demand [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E07 explicitly states that energy losses during conversion of electrical to ultrasonic cavitation are very high and discusses altering matrix chemistry and combining ultrasound with other processes to improve energy efficiency.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06, frequency optimization for maximum PFAS degradation is compound‑specific and not practical for complex PFAS mixtures and real waters [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E07 notes frequency optimization is compound-specific and therefore not practical for mixtures and actual waters.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06 IDW sonication, an inline electricity meter showed 0.4 kWh consumed over 4 h at 1040 W, corresponding to an electricity cost of $0.18/gal at $0.12/kWh [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E04 gives 0.4 kWh over 4 h and calculates cost $0.18/gal at $0.12/kWh.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S01 field sonolysis, ultrasound technology operated in batch mode and displayed pseudo‑first‑order kinetics; increased power density led to greater PFAS degradation [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E08 states ultrasound is a batch process with pseudo‑first‑order kinetics and that increased power density leads to greater PFAS degradation (citing Kewalramani et al.).

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S01, the maximum average PFAS degradation efficiency at 12 h of treatment was 80%, with an order‑of‑magnitude decrease in PFAS concentration in highly contaminated groundwater [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E08 reports maximum average degradation efficiency of 80% at 12 h; S01-E04 describes an order‑of‑magnitude concentration decrease.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S05, EO achieved >99% PFAS removal from contaminated wastewater or RO concentrates in prior studies referenced by the LCA [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-E06 notes that EO achieved >99% PFAS removal from contaminated wastewater and demonstrated efficacy in RO concentrates, citing Nzeribe et al. and Radjenovic et al.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S05, UVAOP (e.g., UV/sulfite) can generate sulfate radicals and initiate PFAS defluorination, achieving high PFAS degradation rates under alkaline conditions [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-E06 states UVAOP can generate sulfate radicals capable of initiating defluorination and that UV/sulfite systems have demonstrated high PFAS degradation rates under alkaline conditions.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In the MIVES-based sustainability evaluation, EO had a sustainability index of 0.90, UVAOP 0.48, and incineration 0.29 [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-E08 provides these SI values.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S05, incineration is modeled as thermal oxidation in oxygen‑abundant environments at 980–1200 °C, with PFAS destruction efficiencies anticipated to exceed 99.9% [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-E05 describes hazardous waste incinerators operating at 980–1200 °C and states organic substances, including PFAS, are expected to be almost completely eliminated (>99.9%).

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S05, EO is described as transforming PFAS to environmentally harmless by‑products through direct electron transfer and radical‑mediated indirect processes, with treatment duration influenced by electrode properties, PFAS concentration, co‑contaminants, efficiency targets, and applied voltage [S05].
claim_assessments.rationale: S05-E05 explains EO direct and indirect processes and notes that duration depends on electrode properties, surface area, PFAS and co‑contaminant concentrations, desired efficiency, and applied voltage.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S01, ultrasound treatment of highly contaminated groundwater achieved an order‑of‑magnitude PFAS decrease with little evidence of problematic PFAS by‑products, and AOF decreased over time [S01].
claim_assessments.rationale: S01-E04 states ultrasound was proven effective for PFAS destruction in highly contaminated GW with little evidence of problematic by‑products, achieving an order‑of‑magnitude concentration decrease and notes a decrease in AOF (supported also by S01-E08).

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S04, defluorination kinetics for PFOA and PFOS in MQ, SW, CW were modeled using (pseudo)-first‑order kinetics based on F⁻ release [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E06 describes defluorination kinetics of PFOA and PFOS in MQ, SW, CW and states that F⁻ concentration was fitted with a (pseudo)-first‑order model using initial PFAS concentration C0.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S04, water quality analyses like TOC were avoided for PFAS‑contaminated samples to prevent potential HF release during those analytical processes, limiting direct carbon‑fate/mineralization assessment.
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E04 states that water quality analysis on example wastes and PFAS‑contaminated GW (e.g., using a TOC analyser) was avoided to prevent HF hazards. The limitation regarding carbon‑fate/mineralization assessment is an inference grounded in this avoidance but not explicit.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06, PFAS degradation rates were directly influenced by ultrasonic power density and were highest in the closed system compared with the open system [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E08 reports pseudo‑first‑order rate constants decreasing with decreasing power density and notes degradation rates were highest in the closed system compared to open systems.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06, PFAS degradation in sonolysis starts with sorption to the acoustic cavity and separation of the headgroup from the carbon‑fluorine chain via pyrolysis, followed by further reactions of the fluorocarbon chain [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E06 states mineralization begins with sorption of PFAS to the cavity, followed by separation of the headgroup from the carbon–fluorine chain; S06-E08 notes the fluorocarbon chain produced by pyrolysis undergoes further reactions.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06, efficient destructive technologies for PFAS are scarce with limited field applicability; ultrasound showed effectiveness for degradation and defluorination of legacy and novel PFAS in real waters, AFFF, and high‑concentration IDW [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E04 concludes that efficient destructive technologies for PFASs are scarce and have limited field applicability, and summarizes that the study demonstrated ultrasound effectiveness for [SOURCE_TEXT_OMITTED sha256=be3ce2e97eca2ed60db6e50f4ace9e7121daee7eb577b72627d8fb9015253b69].

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06 IDW experiments, energy metrics E_EO and E_EM per unit mass PFAS defluorinated/removed are sensitive to whether unidentified PFAS and other degraded organics are included, and energy losses from electrical to cavitation are high [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E02 discusses that including unidentified PFASs and other degraded organics lowers apparent energy per mass and that E_EM is more realistic; S06-E07 notes high energy losses during conversion to cavitation.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S06, if temperature control is not essential, the cooling system can be removed to lower energy consumption associated with cooling [S06].
claim_assessments.rationale: S06-E04 explicitly states that if temperature control is not essential, the cooling component can be removed, lowering energy consumption associated with cooling.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S04, ultrasonication may yield fewer ultrashort‑chain by‑products than other technologies, but operational parameters, energy input, and scalability remain challenges [S04].
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E08 states ultrasonication may yield fewer ultrashort‑chain by‑products compared to other technologies and notes that operational parameters, energy input, and scalability remain challenges.

claim_assessments.claim_text: In S04, experiments on 1000× diluted AFFF and FF are bench‑scale and may not represent treatment performance for undiluted PFAS‑rich streams.
claim_assessments.rationale: S04-E04,E05 describe dilution by 1000× and bench‑scale experiments but do not explicitly discuss representativeness for undiluted waste; the caution is a reasonable inference rather than directly stated.
